Empirical Research Plan: Stock-Price Effects of Discrete Economic Events  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Chosen strategy: Event-study difference-in-differences (event-DiD)

Rationale  
• Event studies exploit the exact calendar date on which new information is released; stock prices should incorporate that information immediately under semi-strong market efficiency.  
• Combining the traditional event-study (abnormal returns in a narrow window) with a panel DiD/event-time specification allows:  
  – causal inference in both short-run (days) and longer-run (weeks/months) horizons;  
  – explicit counterfactual construction and pre-trend tests;  
  – firm and time fixed effects to soak up unobserved heterogeneity and market-wide shocks.  

Alternative designs (IV, RDD) are not naturally available because treatment is discrete and timing is known. A pure DiD without event-time dummies would miss dynamic effects, while an RDD on a running variable is ill-defined.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
• Treated = 1 for firm i on and after the event date τi (e.g., the day of the earnings surprise, merger announcement, or rule change affecting that firm); 0 otherwise.

Control group (counterfactual)  
Option A – Unaffected peer firms in the same 2-digit SIC industry that do not experience the event during the sample window.  
Option B – For robustness, propensity-score or coarsened-exact matching on pre-event size, book-to-market, beta, and momentum to construct a “matched twin” for each treated firm.

Treatment timing / event date  
• τi is the announcement date recorded by Bloomberg/EDGAR/press release.  
• Event window for short-run: [-1, +3] trading days around τi.  
• Longer-run: monthly returns up to +12 months.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends / common shocks: Absent the event, treated firms’ returns would have evolved like those of control firms (conditional on fixed effects).  
  Plausibility: Same-industry and matched controls share fundamental and macro exposures; can be inspected in event-time pre-period (-30 to ‑5).  

A2. No differential information leakage / anticipation: Material information was not (differentially) incorporated prior to τi.  
  Plausibility: SEC Reg FD and listing rules make major leaks costly, but we will test by looking at abnormal returns in days ‑10 to ‑2.  

A3. No spillovers: The event for firm i does not directly alter returns of control firms except through aggregate market moves already absorbed by time fixed effects and factors.  
  Plausibility: Peer effects are possible (e.g., industry-wide re-valuations); we mitigate by excluding very close rivals in robustness checks.

A4. Stable composition: Treated and control firms remain listed and observable throughout the estimation window.  
  Plausibility: Delistings are rare in short windows; we will censor observations at delisting and test sensitivity.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Confounding coincident events (e.g., macro news day).  
  Mitigation: Include market return, Fama-French and momentum factors, and day fixed effects; drop firms whose event day coincides with another firm-specific event.

T2. Selection into treatment: Firms choose announcement dates strategically (e.g., Friday afternoons).  
  Mitigation: Include announcement-day dummies (day-of-week, month-of-year) and show robustness to excluding non-trading-hours announcements.

T3. Cross-sectional heterogeneity in baseline risk (heteroskedasticity, different betas).  
  Mitigation: Compute abnormal returns using each firm’s pre-event market model, and employ cluster-robust SEs at the firm and day level (two-way).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline (executable)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# Load libraries
library(data.table)
library(fixest)
library(lubridate)
library(MatchIt)

# 1. Data loading ---------------------------------------------------
prices <- fread("firm_daily_prices.csv")     # id, date, price, return
events  <- fread("events.csv")               # id, event_date
market  <- fread("market_factors.csv")       # date, mkt_rf, smb, hml, mom, rf

# 2. Merge & variable construction ---------------------------------
setkey(prices, id, date)
setkey(events, id)

# Merge event date
prices <- events[prices]

# Event-time (days relative to announcement)
prices[, event_time := as.numeric(date - event_date)]

# Treatment indicator
prices[, treat := as.integer(!is.na(event_date) & date >= event_date)]

# Abnormal returns via pre-event market model ----------------------
# Estimate beta using days -250 to -30
beta_est <- prices[event_time %between% c(-250,-30),
                   .(alpha = coef(lm(return ~ mkt_rf, data=.SD))[1],
                     beta  = coef(lm(return ~ mkt_rf, data=.SD))[2]),
                   by = id]

prices <- merge(prices, beta_est, by="id", all.x=TRUE)
prices[, abret := return - (alpha + beta*mkt_rf)]

# 3. Matched control sample (optional) -----------------------------
pre_chars <- prices[event_time==-30,
                    .(size = log(market_cap), btm, beta), by=id]

match_out <- matchit(treated ~ size + btm + beta, data=pre_chars, method="nearest")
matched_ids <- rownames(match_out$match.matrix)
prices_matched <- prices[id %in% c(events$id, matched_ids)]

# 4. Main DiD/event-time regression --------------------------------
# Event-time dummies from -10 to +10 (excluding -1 as reference)
for(k in -10:10) prices[, paste0("D",k) := as.integer(event_time==k)]

spec_formula <- as.formula(
  paste("abret ~", 
        paste(paste0("D", -10:10), collapse=" + "),
        "+ i(id) + i(date)"))

did_fit <- feols(spec_formula, data=prices_matched, 
                 cluster = ~id + date)

etable(did_fit)

# 5. Robustness: longer horizon monthly returns --------------------
monthly <- prices[, .(ret_m = prod(1+return)-1), by=.(id, ym = floor_date(date,"month"))]
monthly <- merge(monthly, events[, .(id, event_ym = floor_date(event_date,"month"))], by="id")
monthly[, post12 := as.integer(ym >= event_ym & ym <= event_ym %m+% months(12))]

fit_long <- feols(ret_m ~ post12 + i(id) + i(ym), data=monthly, cluster=~id)
etable(list(short=did_fit, long=fit_long))
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Theory suggests that:
• Positive information events (earnings beats, favorable regulation) → immediate abnormal return of +2 – 5 % over [-1, +3] days.  
• Negative events (earnings miss, unfavorable rule) → –3 – 8 %.  
Longer-run drift is ambiguous; literature often finds partial reversal (~25 % of immediate effect within 3–6 months) due to over-reaction.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (Event-DiD)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1. Parallel pre-trends visually and statistically verified ................. 1  
C2. No anticipation / leakage (no pre-event abnormal returns) ............... 1  
C3. No spillovers to control group .......................................... 0  
C4. Exogenous treatment timing (announcement date) .......................... 0  
C5. Stable sample & no compositional change ................................. 1  

Total = 3 / 5. I judge the design credible but will devote attention to spillovers and endogeneity of timing in robustness analyses.
